title: Statins: Muscle Injury, Interactions, and Adherence
bottomLine: Statins lower LDL cholesterol and cardiovascular risk when appropriately indicated. The PN should reinforce adherence and recognize unexplained muscle pain/weakness, dark urine, major interacting drugs, or hepatic symptoms that require evaluation.
recognize: Myalgia is more common than rhabdomyolysis, but severe weakness with dark urine is concerning.
Myopathy risk rises with selected interacting drugs and patient factors such as advanced age, renal impairment, or untreated hypothyroidism.
priorities: Review new muscle symptoms and interacting medications.
Report severe or persistent weakness, dark urine, or hepatic symptoms.
Reinforce that cardiovascular benefit depends on ongoing use rather than whether the patient can feel the medication working.
assessMonitor: Trend lipid response, medication adherence, muscle symptoms, liver tests when clinically indicated, and interaction changes.
interventions: Support diet, activity, smoking cessation, and other risk-reduction measures alongside medication therapy.
medicationSafety: Atorvastatin has important interactions that can increase myopathy/rhabdomyolysis risk.
Pregnancy requires prompt prescriber review of lipid-lowering therapy.
complications: Acute kidney injury secondary to rhabdomyolysis
redFlags: Rapid renal decline after muscle symptoms
teaching: Report unexplained persistent muscle pain or weakness and provide the prescriber/pharmacist an updated medication list.
delegationScope: Medication administration may be within scope; adverse-effect assessment and therapy changes require licensed-nurse/provider review.
examTrap: Telling a patient to stop a statin permanently for mild nonspecific soreness without assessment of severity, cause, and cardiovascular indication.
oneLinePearl: Statin safety: keep the cardiovascular benefit while catching true muscle toxicity early.

title: Spironolactone: Potassium and Kidney Safety
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Spironolactone blocks aldosterone and conserves potassium. Hyperkalemia is the priority toxicity, especially with kidney dysfunction, potassium supplements/salt substitutes, ACE inhibitors, ARBs, or other potassium-raising exposures.
recognize: Weakness, paresthesias, bradycardia, or dysrhythmia can accompany significant hyperkalemia.
Excess diuresis can also worsen hypotension or renal function.
priorities: Check ordered potassium and renal-function monitoring.
Review potassium supplements and salt substitutes.
Escalate symptomatic hyperkalemia, severe hypotension, or acute kidney injury.
assessMonitor: Trend potassium, creatinine/eGFR, BP, weight/edema, urine output, and symptoms.
interventions: Support the prescribed sodium/fluid plan and avoid unsupervised high-potassium supplements.
medicationSafety: Contraindications include hyperkalemia and Addison disease according to labeling.
Risk increases with impaired renal function and drugs that raise potassium.
teaching: Do not add potassium supplements or potassium-based salt substitutes unless specifically instructed.
delegationScope: Weights and intake/output may be delegated; interpretation of potassium/renal changes requires licensed-nurse judgment.
examTrap: Automatically giving a routine potassium supplement with a potassium-sparing diuretic.
oneLinePearl: Spironolactone spares potassium—so potassium is what you must watch.

title: Nitroglycerin: Chest Pain, Pressure, and PDE-5 Safety
bottomLine: Sublingual nitroglycerin relieves angina by venodilation but can cause profound hypotension. Before administration, assess BP and recent PDE-5 inhibitor or riociguat use; new or persistent ischemic symptoms still require emergency evaluation rather than repeated self-treatment alone.
recognize: Headache, flushing, dizziness, and hypotension are common nitrate effects.
PDE-5 inhibitors can dangerously amplify nitrate-related hypotension.
priorities: Have the patient sit or lie safely and assess BP and symptoms.
Screen for contraindicated PDE-5 inhibitor/riociguat exposure.
Activate the ACS pathway for persistent, severe, or new concerning chest pain.
assessMonitor: Trend BP, heart rate, chest-pain response, dizziness, syncope, and ischemic symptoms.
interventions: Store/administer the product according to formulation instructions and facility policy.
medicationSafety: PDE-5 inhibitors and riociguat are contraindicated with sublingual nitroglycerin because of hypotension risk.
Marked hypotension or preload-dependent states require clinician-specific caution.
teaching: Use nitroglycerin exactly as instructed and seek emergency help for chest pain that is new, severe, persistent, or accompanied by high-risk symptoms.
delegationScope: Medication administration follows state/facility scope; evaluation of acute chest pain cannot be delegated.
examTrap: Giving nitroglycerin before asking about recent sildenafil/tadalafil or checking the patient's blood pressure.
oneLinePearl: Nitro opens veins—check pressure and PDE-5 drugs before the dose.
sourceBasis: FDA/DailyMed Nitroglycerin Sublingual Tablet Prescribing Information

title: Amlodipine: Blood Pressure and Peripheral Edema
bottomLine: Amlodipine lowers blood pressure through arterial vasodilation. Peripheral edema, flushing, dizziness, and hypotension are high-yield effects; ankle edema from amlodipine is not automatically evidence of heart-failure volume overload.
recognize: Dependent ankle edema can occur without pulmonary congestion or rapid weight gain.
Symptomatic hypotension is more concerning than an isolated lower BP in an asymptomatic patient.
priorities: Assess BP, dizziness, falls, edema pattern, weight trend, and heart-failure symptoms.
Distinguish medication-related peripheral edema from generalized congestion before escalating diuretics.
assessMonitor: Trend BP, edema, weight, orthostatic symptoms, angina symptoms, and hepatic impairment when relevant.
interventions: Teach slow position changes and adherence to the prescribed BP plan.
medicationSafety: Symptomatic hypotension is possible, particularly in selected patients with severe outflow obstruction.
Dose titration may need added caution in severe hepatic impairment.
redFlags: Pulmonary edema suggesting a diagnosis beyond simple amlodipine edema
teaching: Report severe dizziness or swelling that is new or worsening; do not stop antihypertensive therapy solely because one reading is normal.
delegationScope: Routine BP measurement may be delegated with reporting parameters; symptom interpretation requires licensed-nurse assessment.
examTrap: Assuming every swollen ankle on amlodipine means the patient needs more diuretic therapy.
oneLinePearl: Amlodipine edema can be vascular, not fluid overload—assess the whole patient.

title: Beta-Lactam Antibiotics: Allergy, Diarrhea, and Completion
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Penicillins and related beta-lactams are common antibiotics; safe administration requires clarifying the actual allergy reaction, watching for anaphylaxis or severe skin reactions, and recognizing significant antibiotic-associated diarrhea rather than labeling every GI symptom as harmless.
recognize: A prior nausea-only history is different from anaphylaxis, angioedema, SJS/TEN, or another severe hypersensitivity reaction.
Persistent or severe diarrhea can represent C. difficile-associated disease.
priorities: Clarify the allergy phenotype before administration when the history is vague.
Stop and escalate airway swelling, wheeze, hypotension, or severe progressive rash.
Report severe/persistent diarrhea, jaundice, or hepatic symptoms.
assessMonitor: Trend infection response, allergy signs, bowel pattern, renal dosing needs, and hepatic symptoms for selected products.
interventions: Obtain cultures before antibiotics when ordered and when doing so will not dangerously delay therapy.
medicationSafety: Amoxicillin-clavulanate is contraindicated after serious hypersensitivity to beta-lactams and after prior drug-associated cholestatic jaundice/hepatic dysfunction according to labeling.
Antibiotic-associated C. difficile illness can begin during or after treatment.
redFlags: Severe watery diarrhea with systemic illness
teaching: Take antibiotics exactly as prescribed and report serious allergy or severe diarrhea rather than self-treating with leftover antibiotics.
delegationScope: Medication administration follows state/facility scope; reaction assessment requires licensed-nurse judgment.
examTrap: Treating every recorded 'penicillin allergy' as identical without asking what actually happened.
oneLinePearl: For beta-lactams, the allergy story matters as much as the allergy label.

title: Azithromycin: QT and Liver Safety
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Azithromycin is a macrolide antibiotic with clinically important QT-prolongation and hepatic risks. The PN should identify patients with existing QT risk, interacting QT-prolonging medications, severe electrolyte abnormalities, or hepatic symptoms before treating the drug as a routine low-risk antibiotic.
recognize: Palpitations, syncope, or new dizziness can signal dysrhythmia in a high-risk patient.
Jaundice, dark urine, severe pruritus, or RUQ symptoms can signal hepatic injury.
priorities: Review QT-risk history and major interacting medications/electrolyte problems.
Report syncope, serious palpitations, or hepatic symptoms promptly.
Monitor clinical response to infection therapy.
assessMonitor: Trend rhythm/ECG when indicated, potassium/magnesium in at-risk patients, liver symptoms, allergy, and GI tolerance.
interventions: Correct significant electrolyte abnormalities when ordered and reinforce adherence to the prescribed regimen.
medicationSafety: Azithromycin can prolong QT and has been associated with torsades de pointes.
Severe hepatotoxicity and serious allergic/skin reactions are recognized warnings.
teaching: Report fainting, severe palpitations, jaundice, or major rash and avoid using leftover antibiotics for future respiratory symptoms.
delegationScope: Reaction and rhythm-risk assessment require licensed-nurse/provider review.
examTrap: Ignoring a markedly low potassium and prolonged QT because azithromycin is commonly prescribed.
oneLinePearl: Common antibiotic does not mean zero risk—azithromycin can affect QT and liver.

title: Doxycycline: Photosensitivity, Administration, and Tooth Development
bottomLine: Doxycycline is a tetracycline antibiotic with important administration and counseling points: photosensitivity can occur, certain minerals/antacids impair absorption, and tetracycline-class exposure during tooth development can discolor teeth. Its use in children or pregnancy is indication-specific and clinician directed—not governed by a simplistic blanket rule.
recognize: An exaggerated sunburn reaction can occur.
Esophageal irritation is more likely when tablets are taken with inadequate water or immediately before lying down.
Calcium, magnesium, aluminum, and iron products can reduce absorption depending on timing/formulation.
priorities: Administer with adequate water and follow product-specific food/mineral instructions.
Teach sun protection.
Report severe headache/visual change, serious rash, or persistent diarrhea.
assessMonitor: Trend GI tolerance, rash/photosensitivity, infection response, and interacting supplements/antacids.
interventions: Separate interacting mineral products according to the prescribed product guidance.
medicationSafety: Tetracycline-class drugs can affect tooth development; age/pregnancy use depends on the infection and current clinical guidance.
C. difficile-associated diarrhea and photosensitivity are recognized warnings.
redFlags: Persistent severe headache with visual symptoms
teaching: Use sun protection, take with sufficient water, and ask how to separate iron/calcium/antacid products.
delegationScope: Routine administration may be within scope; pregnancy/pediatric indication decisions remain prescriber-directed.
examTrap: Giving doxycycline with an iron supplement and immediately putting the patient flat for sleep.
oneLinePearl: Doxycycline teaching: water, stay upright, separate minerals, protect from sun.

title: Fluoroquinolones: Tendon, Nerve, CNS, and Myasthenia Risk
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Fluoroquinolones such as ciprofloxacin have boxed warnings for disabling potentially irreversible tendon, peripheral-nerve, and CNS adverse effects and can worsen myasthenia gravis. New tendon pain, neuropathic symptoms, or significant CNS effects require prompt medication review rather than simply treating the symptom.
recognize: Tendon pain/swelling can precede rupture.
Neuropathy may cause burning, tingling, numbness, pain, or weakness.
CNS effects can include agitation, confusion, hallucinations, insomnia, or seizures in susceptible patients.
priorities: Ask about tendon symptoms, neuropathy, CNS changes, and myasthenia history.
Stop/escalate serious adverse reactions according to the medication plan and labeling.
Avoid unnecessary use for conditions where safer effective alternatives are recommended.
assessMonitor: Trend neurologic symptoms, tendon pain, renal function/dose needs, glucose in susceptible patients, QT risk, and infection response.
interventions: Reduce strenuous activity and obtain prompt evaluation if tendon injury is suspected.
medicationSafety: Fluoroquinolones may exacerbate muscle weakness in myasthenia gravis.
Certain products have important mineral/antacid interactions and QT risks.
teaching: Report tendon pain, new numbness/burning, marked confusion, or new weakness immediately and ask about mineral/antacid separation.
examTrap: Encouraging exercise through Achilles pain that began after starting a fluoroquinolone.
oneLinePearl: Fluoroquinolones can injure tendon, nerve, and CNS—and worsen myasthenia.
sourceBasis: FDA/DailyMed Ciprofloxacin Boxed Warning and Prescribing Information

title: Albuterol: Rescue Bronchodilator and Overuse Signal
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Albuterol is a short-acting beta-2 agonist used for rapid bronchodilation. Tremor and tachycardia are common, but increasing rescue use signals deteriorating airway disease and requires reassessment; paradoxical bronchospasm after inhalation is an emergency medication reaction.
recognize: Expected relief includes improved wheeze, air movement, and dyspnea.
Frequent use can produce tachycardia and transient hypokalemia.
Immediate worsening wheeze after a dose can represent paradoxical bronchospasm.
priorities: Assess respiratory effort and response before/after rescue treatment.
Escalate if relief is poor, rescue doses are increasingly needed, or the patient is tiring.
Stop and urgently evaluate paradoxical bronchospasm.
assessMonitor: Trend respiratory rate, breath sounds, peak flow when used, heart rate, tremor, rescue frequency, and potassium in high-dose acute therapy when indicated.
interventions: Verify inhaler/spacer or nebulizer technique and distinguish rescue from controller medication.
medicationSafety: Albuterol can cause cardiovascular effects and hypokalemia.
It does not replace anti-inflammatory controller therapy when controller therapy is indicated.
teaching: Know which inhaler is the rescue medication and seek reassessment if it is needed more often than usual.
delegationScope: Respiratory treatments may be within LPN/LVN scope by state/facility; response to worsening distress requires licensed-nurse escalation.
examTrap: Reassuring a patient who is using albuterol repeatedly every day because the medication temporarily makes breathing easier.
oneLinePearl: More rescue inhaler use is a disease-warning signal, not proof of good control.
sourceBasis: FDA/DailyMed Albuterol Sulfate Inhalation Prescribing Information

title: Inhaled Corticosteroids: Controller Therapy and Mouth Care
bottomLine: Inhaled corticosteroids reduce airway inflammation and are controller medications—not immediate rescue treatment for acute bronchospasm. Correct technique and rinsing the mouth after use reduce local adverse effects such as oral candidiasis.
recognize: Hoarseness and oral thrush can occur with inhaled corticosteroids.
Poor adherence may present as increasing rescue-inhaler use and exacerbations.
Higher systemic exposure can contribute to adrenal suppression and other steroid effects.
priorities: Verify inhaler/spacer or nebulizer technique and identify rescue versus controller roles.
Inspect the mouth when thrush symptoms occur.
Escalate acute respiratory distress rather than relying on the controller inhaler for immediate relief.
assessMonitor: Trend symptom control, exacerbations, rescue use, oral candidiasis, growth in children when relevant, and systemic steroid effects at higher exposure.
interventions: Rinse the mouth with water without swallowing after inhaled dosing when directed by the product.
Use spacer/holding-chamber devices when appropriate to the inhaler and patient.
medicationSafety: Inhaled corticosteroids are not indicated as sole rescue therapy for acute severe bronchospasm.
Abrupt transition from chronic systemic steroids to inhaled therapy can create adrenal-risk issues and requires clinician direction.
complications: Adrenal suppression with higher systemic exposure
redFlags: Signs of adrenal insufficiency during systemic-steroid transition
teaching: Use the controller every day as prescribed, rinse the mouth afterward, and keep a separate rescue plan for acute symptoms.
delegationScope: Medication administration/teaching reinforcement may be within scope; assessment of uncontrolled asthma requires licensed-nurse/provider review.
examTrap: Giving an inhaled corticosteroid as the only treatment for a patient in an acute severe asthma attack and expecting immediate bronchodilation.
oneLinePearl: Inhaled steroid = prevent inflammation; albuterol = rescue bronchospasm.
sourceBasis: FDA/DailyMed Budesonide and Fluticasone Inhalation Prescribing Information
